title: Do you need to lift heavy to get big?
summary: NH says 'lift heavy to get big' is true but incomplete: leverages matter more than muscle size for strength, and hypertrophy comes from tonnage (total weight moved). 'Heavy' is personal and rep-dependent; train within roughly 60-90% of max (about 2-15 controlled reps), avoid junk volume at both extremes, and rotate rep schemes.

claims.claim: 'Lifting heavy makes you bigger' is true in a sense but lacks key information; mass moves mass, yet leverages matter more than muscle size for strength.
Someone with arms reaching past the knees would be a deadlift world-record holder thanks to a tiny range of motion, with no need for big muscles.
Good leverages multiply muscle strength, so a little added muscle on a well-leveraged lifter beats a lot added on a poorly-leveraged one.
Natural bodybuilders shouldn't assume getting stronger always means getting bigger; someone can squat 450 lbs without big legs if their leverages are better.
Hypertrophy occurs through tonnage, the total weight moved in a workout; more tonnage means more fiber damage and growth.
It's better to do 10 reps with 315 than 2 reps with 350.
Staying stuck in one rep scheme eventually lets a lifter progressing heavier sets outpace you in volume, so rotate rep schemes.
Seek heavy weight within whatever rep range you want to stimulate; NH keeps his heavy squat work at 4-8 reps at all times.
The bulk of your work should be volume work, which NH defines as above 6 reps; 4x6-10 or 4x8-12 builds much more tonnage than 4x5.
You define what heavy is; bowing to others' standards pushes you into ever-lower reps, reducing volume, hypertrophy and eventually strength.
Reps should always be challenging but never damaging.
Junk volume is a spectrum: too light does nothing, but too heavy (grinding, broken form, rushed negatives) is worse because it also risks injury.
The right intensity bracket is about 60-90% of max: roughly 2-4 controlled reps at the top end up to about 15 at the bottom; natural bodybuilders should live inside it.
Heaviness depends on reps: 205 lbs for 12 on flat bench is heavy for NH, as is 265 for 2.
Heaviness also depends on position in the workout: 185 lbs close-grip bench for 10 is heavy at the end of his session; as an opener it would be 205-215.
